accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (DfE 2023) for 3 and 4 year olds (plant seeds and care for growing plants, life cycle of a plant), Year 1 plants (basic structure: roots, stem, leaves, flowers) and Year 2 plants (seeds and bulbs grow into mature plants; need water, light and a suitable temperature). Germination needs water, warmth and air; the radicle emerges first and is gravitropic; beans germinate in the dark with pale etiolated shoots, while lettuce is noted as a light-needing exception.

misconceptions.evidence: Tackles the beliefs small children actually hold about seeds: that the green shoot comes out first (root-or-shoot prediction and the leaf tag), that a seed needs sunshine to start (dark cupboard prediction shows it sprouts pale), that an upside down bean grows the wrong way (jar rotation), that a cold wet seed will still grow (fridge pot), and that seeds come from soil rather than from a grown plant (life story prediction and the jump tag).

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagseed lab is the only one where a child pushes a bean into a pot and pours water on it, scrubs a day slider to watch a curving root and shoot grow inside a glass jar from three bean orientations, carries a wet pot to a window, a cupboard or a fridge, drops part names onto a living seedling, and builds a four-card seed-to-plant strip. The 6-token shingle gate passed against every other flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each step adds one idea on top of the last: planting and watering, then which part emerges first and which way it heads, then the conditions that start germination, then the names root, shoot and leaf on the plant the child grew, then the full cycle back to seeds. Every finish line states the rule in words a four year old can repeat, such as 'The root comes out first and turns down'.

predictions.evidence: Three locked-in guesses come before any evidence appears: root or shoot first (the shoot is tempting because it is the part we see above the soil), whether a wet seed in a dark cupboard sprouts (tempting no, because plants need sun), and where new seeds come from (tempting the soil or the shop). The reveal compares the child's answer with what the jar, the cupboard pot or the big plant shows.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The five question challenge gives a different reply to each wrong pick: choosing a leaf first explains the root must drink first, choosing a flower explains flowers come last, choosing light explains seeds start in dark soil, choosing dry or cold explains water and warmth, and choosing up for the root or jump for new seeds each gets a short reason. Correct answers restate the fact rather than just saying well done.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs score Flesch-Kincaid grade 0.6 with short sentences and words like root, shoot, wake up and lunch box; adult text scores 9.8, inside the family target, and introduces germinate, radicle and seedling with plain glosses. Lab prompts are mostly under eight words, and every drag target also carries a large labelled button for children who cannot drag yet.

no_filler.evidence: There is no warm-up text or empty praise: the key idea moves straight from what a seed is to what wakes it, the order of root and shoot, and the cycle. The family tip is a concrete bean-in-a-jar activity with two questions to ask, and the adult section is spent on curriculum statements, exact vocabulary, the common mistakes and what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: Walked through on an iPhone 13 viewport and a 1200 pixel desktop: all six steps render, five tasks complete through Show me, and the challenge is visible. Screenshots in light and dark themes show the pot, jar, three spot cards and four life cards fitting the width; the longest card label was shortened to 'tiny root' after it touched the card edge on a phone.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no violations in either theme on desktop or phone. The canvas has an aria-label and every drag has a button twin (plant, water, sunny window, dark cupboard, cold fridge, part names, life cards), so the whole lab works by keyboard or screen reader taps. Colours come from the theme palette with dark text on light card fills, and the status messages are spoken through the live region.
